articles.title: Sleep loss reduces muscle endurance by rewiring brain networks, study finds
articles.summary: Getting less than four hours of sleep severely reduces physical endurance, but not because your muscles tire out faster. A new study shows that sleep deprivation forces the brain to inefficiently rewire its neural networks, triggering premature physical exhaustion.

articles.title: Psilocybin therapy has mostly reached the well-off. A small Oregon study tested a cheaper group model for low-income patients
articles.summary: Most psychedelic research has drawn well-off participants. In a first-of-its-kind Oregon study, 19 low-income adults with depression completed group psilocybin therapy, and their average depression scores fell by more than half.

articles.title: Expanding Attention: A Taylor-Series Route to Linear-Time Transformers with a Fixed Number of Recurrent States
articles.summary: arXiv:2610.20637v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We expand the exponential kernel of attention into a truncated Taylor series of $n$ terms and factorize each term into a tensor-power inner product, which collapses the causal history into exactly $n$ recurrent states, each updated by one rank-one outer product per token and independent of context length $N$. The recursion is lossless with respect to the truncated kernel ($2.2 \times 10^{-16}$ in float64), and the states are additive across chunks ($5.7 \times 10^{-14}$), so prefill admits a parallel scan. Measured exponents are $t \propto N^{2.2

articles.title: Hiring bias against transgender women depends on both identity and appearance, field experiment suggests
articles.summary: In a field experiment involving more than 10,000 job applications in Germany, trans women who disclosed their identity or had male-coded facial features each received about 10 percent fewer positive responses from employers. When both signals were present, the penalty jumped to 32 percent.

articles.title: Many people judge candidates and policies by a single deciding feature, new research suggests
articles.summary: Many survey methods assume people weigh every feature of a candidate or policy. New research suggests most don’t: mental shortcuts dominated, and the strategy people used often shifted from one issue to the next.

articles.title: Yale scientists discover how stress changes the brain to make memories stronger
articles.summary: Yale scientists have uncovered how the stress hormone cortisol helps the brain turn emotional experiences into stronger, longer-lasting memories. The discovery reveals that stress can reshape communication between brain networks involved in emotion and memory, potentially explaining why certain moments are so difficult to forget.

articles.title: Scientists may have overlooked a hidden Alzheimer's culprit for decades
articles.summary: For decades, scientists have focused on amyloid beta as a major culprit behind Alzheimer’s disease, spending billions of dollars developing treatments that have often delivered disappointing results. Now, researchers at UC Santa Cruz are drawing attention to a largely overlooked peptide called P3 that could also play a role in the disease. Previously believed to be harmless, P3 can form harmful-looking protein clumps even faster than amyloid beta and may also damage brain cells.

articles.title: Oxytocin amplifies negative childhood memories for anxiously attached adults
articles.summary: Oxytocin is often called the "love hormone," but new research shows it can actually amplify negative childhood memories for people who experience relationship anxiety. The hormone appears to heighten our sensitivity to social cues, rather than simply boosting affection.

articles.title: Some adults’ brains look older than their age, and gut biology may be part of the picture
articles.summary: Some adults’ brains look “older” than their age long before old age. In a study of 1,400+ people aged 18 to 65, older-looking brain patterns were linked to somewhat weaker working memory, more depressive symptoms, and subtle gut differences.

articles.title: Family genetics study questions the role of genetic nurture in ADHD
articles.summary: A large study of families suggests that a child's own DNA drives their ADHD traits by mid-childhood, finding no robust evidence that parents' genetics indirectly shape these behaviors through the household environment.

articles.title: Your job says little about what you want in a partner, study suggests
articles.summary: Does a nurse want a different kind of partner than an engineer? In a study of nearly 2,000 adults across seven countries, the industry people worked in had almost no link to what they prioritized in a partner.
